PART 7 — The Gospel's Vocabulary: Relational and Cultural Lens

Scripture explains one saving reality using pictures from different social worlds: the royal court, the courtroom, the slave market, the temple, the household. Each picture answers a different question — and each leads to union. Misunderstandings often arise when one picture is made the whole story.

7.1 Term Cards

GOSPEL (good news)  εὐαγγέλιον euangelion · בָּשַׂר basar
WorldA herald's announcement of victory or a king's accession. In the Roman world, euangelia proclaimed the emperor's birth or accession (a famous inscription from Priene, c. 9 BC, calls Augustus's birthday the beginning of "good news"). Isaiah's herald announces "Your God reigns" (Isa 40:9; 52:7).
Misread asA script for securing a place in heaven; or private spiritual advice.
Relational readingThe announcement that the true King has acted in the Son to bring humanity home into His reign and family — first news about who God is and what He has done, then an invitation.
TextsIsa 52:7; Mark 1:14-15; Rom 1:1-4; 1 Cor 15:1-4
GRACE  χάρις charis · חֵן chen (favour) · חֶסֶד chesed (covenant love)
WorldIn Greco-Roman life, charis was the favour or gift that bound patron and client in gratitude and loyalty. In Hebrew, favour "in the eyes of" someone (Gen 6:8) and covenant kindness.
Misread asAn abstract commodity ("unmerited favour") that God dispenses; or a licence to ignore holiness.
Relational readingThe Giver giving Himself: gift and relationship together. Grace is how the Triune life flows toward us ("grace upon grace," John 1:16) — and it trains us (Titus 2:11-12), rather than excusing sin.
TextsJohn 1:14-17; Eph 2:4-8; Titus 2:11-14; 2 Cor 8:9
FAITH  πίστις pistis · אֱמוּנָה emunah (from 'aman, to be firm, reliable)
WorldFaithfulness, reliability, trust. In Roman culture fides was the mutual trust that held patron and client together.
Misread asIntellectual agreement; or "believing hard enough" to move God.
Relational readingResting weight on a trustworthy Person — receiving what He has done. "The righteous shall live by his faithfulness (emunah)" (Hab 2:4). Debated: whether pistis Christou (Rom 3:22; Gal 2:16, 20) means faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ (or both).
TextsHab 2:4; Rom 1:17; Gal 2:20; Heb 11:1, 6
REPENTANCE  μετάνοια metanoia · שׁוּב shuv
WorldShuv: a physical about-turn, a return. Metanoia: a change of mind that changes direction (distinct from mere regret, metamelomai).
Misread asSelf-punishment, grovelling or feeling terrible.
Relational readingTurning toward a Father who is already running toward you: "God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance" (Rom 2:4). (See the earlier forgiveness study.)
TextsLuke 15:17-20; Rom 2:4; 2 Cor 7:10; Acts 3:19
FORGIVENESS  ἄφεσις aphesis · נָשָׂא nasa · סָלַח salach · χαρίζομαι charizomai
WorldDebt-cancellation and release of captives (the Jubilee, Lev 25); lifting a burden and carrying it away.
Misread asGod's mood changing after we grovel; or "forgive and forget."
Relational readingA release God has already given (2 Cor 5:19; Col 2:13-14), received in trust and passed on (Eph 4:32). Distinct from repentance and reconciliation (see the earlier study).
TextsLuke 4:18; Matt 18:27; Col 2:13-14; Eph 4:32
JUSTIFICATION / VINDICATION  δικαιόω dikaioo · צָדַק tsadaq (Hiphil: to declare righteous)
WorldA courtroom word: the judge acquits the one in the right ("justify the righteous and condemn the wicked," Deut 25:1); in Israel's covenant world it also means public vindication of the wronged (Isa 50:8-9).
Misread asA cold legal fiction ("treated as if you hadn't sinned") detached from relationship; or a one-time transaction that changes nothing.
Relational readingGod's public declaration over a person: "The charge is dismissed; you are in the right standing — mine." Jesus himself was "vindicated (edikaiothe) by the Spirit" (1 Tim 3:16) and raised "for our justification" (Rom 4:25); in union his vindication is shared (Rom 8:33-34). It ends the need to justify ourselves (see the earlier study on self-justification).
DebatedReformed (imputed righteousness), "New Perspective" (covenant membership), Catholic and Orthodox (transformative), and union-centred readings (vindication in Christ) emphasise different aspects.
TextsDeut 25:1; Rom 3:24-26; 4:25; 5:1; 8:33-34; Gal 2:16; 1 Tim 3:16
RIGHTEOUSNESS  צְדָקָה tsedaqah · δικαιοσύνη dikaiosyne
WorldRight relationship and the faithful conduct that fits it. When Judah says of Tamar, "She is more righteous than I" (Gen 38:26), he means she kept the family obligation he had neglected. Of God, righteousness is His covenant faithfulness and saving action (Ps 98:2-3; Isa 51:5-8).
Misread asMoral flawlessness against a rulebook; or only God's punitive justice.
Relational readingBeing as one ought to be in relation — rightly related to God and others, and living in the shape of that relation. "The righteousness of God" (Rom 1:17; 3:21) is His faithful putting-right of the world; in Christ we are given a share of it ("that in him we might become the righteousness of God," 2 Cor 5:21 — which scholars debate).
TextsGen 15:6; 38:26; Ps 98:2; Rom 1:17; 3:21-22; 2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9
GLORY  כָּבוֹד kavod (from kaved, "to be heavy") · δόξα doxa (classical: opinion, reputation, esteem)
WorldKavod: weight, substance, honour — a person of "weight" has glory; to "give glory" is to acknowledge someone's true weight. Doxa in ordinary Greek meant opinion, reputation or esteem; the Greek Old Testament chose it to translate kavod, joining "weighty presence" with "good reputation, approval."
Misread asBright light only; or God's ego needing praise.
Relational readingThe weight and beauty of a person made known and honoured. Father and Son glorify one another (John 17:1, 5), and the Son shares that glory with us "that they may be one as we are one" (17:22). Humans were made for it (Ps 8:5) and hunger for approval; John sets the glory of people against the glory of God — approval versus approval (John 5:41-44; 12:43). Hence "testifying" and "approval" are genuine shades of doxa.
TextsExod 33:18-23; Ps 8:5; John 1:14; 5:41-44; 12:43; 17:1-5, 22-24; Rom 3:23; 2 Cor 3:18
SALVATION  יָשַׁע yasha · σῴζω sozo
WorldYasha is often linked to the idea of being brought into a wide, spacious place out of narrowness and distress (compare Ps 18:19). Sozo covers rescue from death, illness and danger, and making whole.
Misread as"Fire insurance": a ticket out of hell concerned only with the afterlife.
Relational readingRescue into spacious, whole, shared life with God, begun now and completed in resurrection: "your faith has made you well" (Mark 5:34, sozo); "today salvation has come to this house" (Luke 19:9).
TextsMark 5:34; Luke 19:9-10; John 3:17; Rom 10:9-13; Eph 2:8
REDEMPTION  גָּאַל ga'al (kinsman-redeemer) · פָּדָה padah · ἀπολύτρωσις apolutrosis · λύτρον lutron
WorldThe family and the slave market: a relative buys back a family member sold into debt (Lev 25:25-49; Ruth 3-4, Boaz as go'el); God redeems Israel from slavery (Exod 6:6).
Misread asA payment to the devil; or a cold commercial transaction.
Relational readingA kinsman acts: the Son became our brother (Heb 2:11-17) to bring His family out of bondage — and the goal is homecoming: "to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption" (Gal 4:4-5).
TextsLev 25:25; Ruth 4:9-10; Exod 6:6; Mark 10:45; Gal 4:4-5; Eph 1:7; Heb 2:14-17
ATONEMENT AND RECONCILIATION  כָּפַר kaphar · ἱλαστήριον hilasterion · καταλλαγή katallage
WorldThe Temple and the Day of Atonement (Lev 16): blood cleanses sanctuary and people, restoring access to God's presence (kaphar: cover, wipe away, ransom). Katallage comes from exchange and the repair of friendship.
Misread asA third party appeasing an angry God, as in pagan placation; or a wordplay on "at-one-ment" alone.
Relational readingGod Himself provides the means and the Person: "God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself" (2 Cor 5:19). The appeal "be reconciled to God" (5:20) is a passive imperative: receive what has been done.
DebatedChristians hold several models — penal substitution, Christus Victor, moral influence, recapitulation/union — often together; hilasterion (Rom 3:25) is rendered propitiation, expiation or mercy seat (compare Heb 9:5).
TextsLev 16; Rom 3:25; 5:10-11; 2 Cor 5:18-21; Col 1:19-22; Heb 9:11-14; 1 John 2:2
ADOPTION  υἱοθεσία huiothesia ("placing as a son")
WorldIn Roman practice an adopted son took the family name and full standing as heir (scholars debate how closely Paul follows Roman law). Behind it lies Israel as God's "son" (Exod 4:22; Hos 11:1).
Misread asA second-class status or a legal technicality.
Relational readingFull family standing and a share in the Son's inheritance, with the Spirit of the Son in our hearts crying "Abba" — the relational goal toward which redemption and justification lead (Eph 1:5).
TextsRom 8:14-17; Gal 4:4-7; Eph 1:4-6
HOLINESS / SANCTIFICATION  קָדַשׁ qadash · ἁγιάζω hagiazo
WorldTo be set apart for someone — a vessel, priest or people dedicated to God; belonging before behaviour.
Misread asMoral perfection achieved by effort; or looking "religious."
Relational readingBelonging to God and being formed into His likeness: Paul calls the messy Corinthians "sanctified in Christ Jesus" (1 Cor 1:2) — a status and a process.
TextsLev 20:26; John 17:17-19; 1 Cor 1:2; 6:11; 1 Thess 5:23
SIN  חָטָא chata (miss the mark) · עָוֹן avon (twistedness) · פֶּשַׁע pesha (rebellion) · ἁμαρτία hamartia
WorldArchery and path imagery: missing, bending, breaking away; breach of covenant.
Misread asA list of rule violations with God as scorekeeper.
Relational readingA breach of trust and love — living from the lie of separation. "Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin" (Rom 14:23); the Spirit convicts "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me" (John 16:9). Sin is the condition (living as if apart) that produces sins.
TextsGen 3; Ps 51:4; Rom 3:23; 14:23; John 16:9
PEACE  שָׁלוֹם shalom · εἰρήνη eirene
WorldWholeness, well-being and right relationships; the everyday greeting.
Misread asThe absence of conflict; or an inner-calm technique.
Relational readingRestored wholeness with God and each other: "peace with God" (Rom 5:1), Christ's own peace (John 14:27) — and Christ "himself is our peace" (Eph 2:14): a Person, not a feeling.
TextsIsa 9:6; John 14:27; Rom 5:1; Eph 2:14-18
LOVE  אָהַב ahav · חֶסֶד chesed · ἀγάπη agape
WorldCommitted, self-giving, covenant love. Agape was a relatively uncommon word in everyday Greek that the biblical writers took up for God's love.
Misread asA mood or sentiment; or being nice.
Relational readingThe Triune life itself: "God is love" (1 John 4:8, 16); the Father's love for the Son (John 17:24, 26) is the love in which we are invited to abide (John 15:9).
TextsJohn 15:9; 17:26; Rom 5:5, 8; 1 John 4:7-21

7.2 Why So Many Misreadings?

  • One metaphor made the whole story. Reading only the courtroom ("verdict") makes the gospel cold; only the temple ("blood") can make God sound angry; only the slave market ("price") raises "to whom?"; the household and union complete them.
  • Modern words replace ancient ones. "Righteousness" becomes moral perfection; "glory" becomes brightness; "faith" becomes opinion.
  • The relational layer is lost when each term is treated as a transaction instead of a stage in a relationship.

PART 8 — Summary, Practices, FAQ and Sources

8.1 Ten Statements

  1. God is, in Himself, a communion of love: Father, Son and Spirit in mutual indwelling.
  2. Humanity was made to share that life; participation is the purpose, not a plan B.
  3. The master lie is separation: "you are outside, and it is up to you."
  4. Alienation is real as experience, hostility of mind and broken trust; it is not God's withdrawal.
  5. In the incarnation, cross, resurrection and gift of the Spirit, God has accomplished union.
  6. New birth is the Spirit's gift of life and awakening — "you will know."
  7. Christ in us is both given and, in the home-making sense, received in love and trust (John 14:20, 23).
  8. Justification, righteousness, glory, redemption, atonement and adoption are pictures from different worlds of one reality: union.
  9. Living from union changes identity, shame, relationships, prayer, suffering and mission.
  10. It does not replace professional care, honest community or growth over time.

8.2 A Simple Daily Practice

MomentPractice
MorningRead one "with" text (Eph 2:5-6; Gal 2:20; Col 3:3). Say: "I am in him and he is in me."
When the lie speaksName it: "This is the separation lie — 'you're outside; prove yourself.'" Breathe out. Return: "I am held."
EveningPray Eph 1:17-19 and 3:16-19: that the eyes of the heart be enlightened and that Christ be at home in your heart.
WeeklyShare one honest thing with a safe person; receive the response as the family speaking.

8.3 FAQ

QuestionAnswer
Is "separation is a lie" saying sin doesn't matter?No. Sin and alienation are real and costly (Part 3.3); the claim is that they are not the final truth about our relationship with God, who has acted in Christ.
Does union mean everyone is saved?Not necessarily. Christians who hold inclusion readings differ on final outcomes; Part 3.3's purple box lays out the disagreement. This study does not settle it.
Is perichoresis in the Bible?The word is not; the reality (mutual indwelling) is, especially in John.
Is the Trinity a dance?As a metaphor of joyful mutual giving, yes; as the Greek meaning of the word, no.
If I'm already in Christ, do I still need to be "born again"?Yes, in the sense John 3 describes: the Spirit's gift of life and awakening. The readings in Part 5.3 differ on whether it is the start of union or the awakening into it.
Why do some terms (justification, atonement) seem cold?Because a single metaphor was made the whole; read each within the household of union (Part 7).

8.4 Sources and Limits

Word studies reflect standard lexicons and commentary; nuances differ. On perichoresis: the word is post-biblical (Gregory of Nazianzus and Maximus the Confessor for Christ's natures; John of Damascus for the Trinity), derived from peri + chorein; the link to choreia (dance) is regarded by standard references as a modern wordplay, though a fruitful image (Moltmann, Volf, Zizioulas, Kruger). On mone: it occurs only in John 14:2 and 14:23. The Priene inscription, Roman adoption practice, yasha's "spaciousness," and agape's relative rarity are commonly cited background; scholars qualify each. Theology: the union-centred reading summarised here is the relational-gospel framework of this series, not a consensus of all Christians; Kruger's views are represented only at the level of that framework, with no verbatim quotation. Christians disagree on the scope of union, the meaning of new birth, justification, atonement and the final outcome for those who never awaken; those places are marked. Cases are composites. This is not clinical or counselling advice; for anxiety, trauma or depression please involve a qualified professional alongside spiritual care.
